data.title: Weapons of the Nitrans in the time of Great Moravia
data.excerpt: A complete set of armament was extremely costly: the equipment of an elite warrior — helmet, body armour, sword and scabbard, greaves, shield with spear, spurs and a horse with its harness — was worth about 50 cows. Most riders and foot soldiers therefore fought with basic weapons only, and the graves with militaria show how unevenly the sword, the axe, the spear, the knife and the bow were distributed.

children.text: A complete set of armament was a very costly matter, and in Great Moravia it can be reckoned with only in the milieu of the ruling classes. The armament of an elite warrior — that is, a helmet, body armour, a sword with its scabbard, greaves, a shield with a spear, spurs and a horse with its harness — could be worth about 50 cows. Most riders and foot soldiers therefore fought with basic weapons only. According to the way they were used and their shape, weapons can be divided into cutting weapons (the sword, the combat knife, the sabre), thrown weapons (the spear, the javelin), percussive weapons (the axe) and missile weapons (the bow and arrow).

When reconstructing the life of a Great Moravian, or of a group of people (a family, a settlement, a hamlet, a craftsmen’s, merchants’ or military retinue and others), it is useful to know how to match civilian and military dress, and dress appropriate to social status.
The sword

The swords of the Great Moravian period are classed among the so-called Carolingian swords (mid-8th century – mid-11th century). This is a medieval sword with a flattened, fully developed pommel and a central lightening groove, the so-called “blood” groove, on a blade more than 70 cm long. The standard length of swords in the territory of present-day Slovakia at this time was around 90 cm, and the width of the blade at the guard about 6 cm. The total weight of the sword was around one kilogram.

children.text: In graves with militaria they account for a statistical share of 6.8%. They were used mainly by the cavalry, but graves containing a sword without any equestrian attributes are documented as well. The sword found at Závada, for instance, is interesting and exceptional. It belonged to a man aged 30–40. It is a type X sword with surviving remains of a strap with mounts. Like the sword from Dolné Krškany, it was evidently worn across the shoulder. It had been placed in a wooden scabbard. It is a long (93 cm) and heavy (1,430 g after cleaning) sword. Compared with other swords from Great Moravia its guard is long (16 cm), especially in comparison with other type X swords, where the length of the guard ranges between 10 and 14 cm. It is precisely type X that archaeologists find most frequently in Slovakia. The unifying features of this type of sword include a semicircular pommel and a longer straight guard of quadrangular section. The high frequency of their occurrence may have been influenced by the simplicity of the form and the undemanding nature of its production. A good-quality sword was expensive and belonged in the hands of professional warriors. Several examples of Great Moravian swords have been found in Slovakia, and the circumstances of the finds almost always indicate that the person buried belonged to a higher social stratum. Swords were found exclusively in male graves, mostly with above-standard grave goods. Female and child graves are entirely absent. Spurs are almost the rule in graves with swords. Axes, daggers and knives also occur frequently.

Sword finds from the territory of present-day Slovakia testify to the high artistic and craft skill of the smiths who made these noble weapons. The smiths who produced the swords must have been experienced, and production probably took place in specialised workshops. Naturally, what was needed above all was a sufficient supply of good-quality metal and, not least, skill, experience and enough time.

blocks.alt: Weapons of the Nitrans in the time of Great Moravia

children.text: The scholarly community holds that in earlier times the Slavs imported swords, because they did not know them and therefore did not make them. It is likely that it was mainly the blades that were imported, while the pommels and guards of swords were also a domestic product. Later, especially in the time of Great Moravia, the production of blades (and, of course, of the remaining parts of the sword) was already commonly carried out at home.

blocks.alt: Weapons of the Nitrans in the time of Great Moravia

children.text: First and foremost the sword was a symbol of power, because not just anyone could afford one, and so these weapons were owned only by the wealthiest. Making a sword was demanding not only financially but also in terms of time. The long double-edged sword (described as Frankish, Carolingian or Norman) developed from the older sword known as the “spatha”. From the 8th century the Frankish sword gradually became the most important weapon in this region. Its numbers were not great, which holds true for every phase of the Early Middle Ages. It was not used in combat to any great extent and functioned primarily as the symbol of power already mentioned. In the territory of present-day Slovakia swords gained in importance from the end of the 8th century. It was then that very high-quality swords from Frankish workshops in the Rhineland reached the Slavs (despite the bans imposed by the Frankish Empire). These swords were often made using the pattern-welded damascus technique (which increased their strength and resilience), they bore the marks of the swordsmiths who made them (the most important swordsmith of the period was the Rhenish master Ulfberth) and they had a decorated grip and pommel. From the second half of the 9th century local sword production can also be considered in Great Moravia, both of simple types and of high-quality imitations of Frankish swords.

children.text: The axe

It is the most common weapon of the Slavs; in the assemblage of graves with militaria in Slovakia it accounts for 55%. The finds can be divided into three basic types. The commonest type was the “bearded axe” (74%), whose standard length ranges from 15 to 17 cm. Less frequent were “narrow axes” (19.2%). Their length varied between 14 and 17 cm. “Broad axes” (6.8%) were represented to the same extent as swords; their length lies in the range 13.5–16 cm. These percentages surprisingly agree with the finds from neighbouring Moravia, so we may argue that the inhabitants here applied the same criteria for placing axes in graves. Rare wooden hafts 70–90 cm long have also survived from Mikulčice; the axe was mounted on them in much the same way as a pickaxe is today. Axes on longer hafts, the so-called danax, are entirely absent in the territory of present-day Slovakia.

blocks.caption: A bearded axe from Diviacka Nová Ves
blocks.alt: A bearded axe from Diviacka Nová Ves

children.text: Specialists regard most axe finds from graves as weapons, although their use in work and craft cannot be ruled out. A purely military use applies with greater certainty to bearded axes, and indeed to all axes with a hammer poll. Injuries caused by them are attested on skeletal material.

The axe could hardly be missing from any household, and by early medieval standards it was the most suitable solution for the lower social strata in the event of combat. It was used mainly by the infantry, although we have evidence of several cases of its use by Great Moravian cavalry. In combat it matches the sword: on a long haft, and thanks to the physical properties of its construction and the distribution of its weight, it has enormous penetrating power. Despite its relatively low weight — 350–500 g — its high-set centre of gravity and fairly narrow edge caused fatal injuries. Compared with a sword, an axe requires 50–75% less iron and far less work to make. Knives were often found in graves with axes, and sometimes spurs. Other weapons are very rare.

blocks.alt: Weapons of the Nitrans in the time of Great Moravia

children.text: The spear

Spears are among the oldest kinds of weapon in the whole history of humankind. In the assemblage of graves with militaria in Slovakia the spear accounts for a share of 12.7%. It was widespread among less wealthy warriors, for the same reason as the axe, yet it was also a powerful weapon in the hands of riders. Earlier written mentions, however, speak of a much wider use of this weapon among the Slavs. In the hands of foot soldiers it is an excellent weapon against cavalry. The classic Great Moravian spear has a leaf-shaped head 26–33 cm long; rare but also interesting is the type of spear with lateral wings, the head of which exceeds 40 cm in length. In battle the spear was used in the first phase, when the formations were still far apart. For close combat spears are of little use. They are effective in a mêlee only when drawn up in the rear ranks. A spear used in foot combat reached a length equal to the height of the warrior or greater, although some heads are found in graves at shoulder height. The usual length of the shafts was thus 160–200 cm among foot warriors. Riders evidently used much longer shafts. These weapons could alternatively have been used for hunting as well, but the data from graves with spears confirm overall a close link between the buried individual and warfare. Knives were frequently represented in the graves, and everyday items are not negligible either. Spurs, buckets and axes also occurred occasionally.
The knife

It was a basic part of every person’s equipment — men, women and also children — regardless of age or of membership of a social stratum or craft. It must, however, be seen both as a weapon and as an item of everyday use and a tool. Specialists regard a knife longer than 15.1 cm as a weapon, while short knives (up to 10 cm) and medium-length knives (10.1–15 cm) are considered everyday items. Medium-length knives dominate in the graves. Among graves in which other everyday items and tools were also found, knives make up 86.3%. In the assemblage of all graves with funerary goods the figure is 38.4%. They were suspended in wooden, leather or textile sheaths, often combined with metal. Wooden sheaths, however, clearly dominate. The use of textile materials for this purpose is attested by corroded textile impressions in the metal. In the territory of present-day Slovakia it is almost exclusively single-edged knives that appear in the function of weapons. The (long) combat knife accounts for 21.5% of all knives. Its military use may also be indicated by the fact that it was worn differently, that is, suspended on the left side of the body. Smaller knives have no dominant side.
The bow and arrow

The existence of bows among the Slavs in the territory of present-day Slovakia is attested by finds of arrowheads, but also by bone plates from reflex bows, as early as the 7th century. Arrowheads were also given to female and child graves, as well as to the graves of juveniles; in 20% of cases the sex could not be determined. In graves with militaria they account for a statistical share of 55.8%. Archers’ graves, however, only rarely contained other weapons.

blocks.alt: Weapons of the Nitrans in the time of Great Moravia

children.text: Archers made up predominantly the defensive infantry formations. On the battlefield, too, they provided covering fire before the cavalry advanced. Typical is the simple, long self bow, made of flexible yew, ash, dogwood or oak wood. They were 150–190 cm long, with notches at the ends to seat the bowstring. It is possible that the bows were reinforced in the middle, but the only find of a bow from the territory of Great Moravia, from Mikulčice, does not confirm this. The combination of a considerably long bow and an arrow length of around 80 cm allowed a range of more than 200 m. The lethal effect of the shot can be estimated for this distance, but the range could have been much greater. A. Ruttkay estimates it at as much as 400 m. The thickness of the wooden shafts was a little under 1 cm and the arrowheads were fitted onto them by means of sockets. The bowstring could have been made of sinew or of twisted hemp or flax fibres. In shooting it was drawn with two fingers, and the accuracy of the flight was ensured by three flights.

blocks.caption: Fragments of a Great Moravian bow from Mikulčice
blocks.alt: Fragments of a Great Moravian bow from Mikulčice

children.text: Arrows were carried in a quiver, and the finds suggest that they were also placed in graves inside quivers. The archer wore the quiver on his back, running along the arm and elbow down to the pelvis on the right side, or along the elbow and pelvis down to the knee on the left side of the body. No preserved quivers, however, have been found in Slavic graves from the territory of present-day Slovakia. The capacity of the quiver determined the warrior’s striking power. The arrowheads in the graves indicate that he could carry 12 to 24 arrows with him.

blocks.caption: A depiction of a Great Moravian archer on a disc mount from Mikulčice
blocks.alt: A depiction of a Great Moravian archer on a disc mount from Mikulčice

children.text: From the pre-Great Moravian period, from the territory of present-day Slovakia, we also have finds of arrows with small holes of unknown function. One suggestion is a form of psychological effect of whistling arrows, another the use of the holes for tying on incendiary substances. It is more likely, however, that the head was strengthened by being bound through the holes, given its considerable cost.

In the south of the territory of present-day Slovakia composite (reflex) bows have also been found, probably survivals from the Avar Khaganate — yet the archaeological finds as a whole suggest that Avar influence north of the Danube was only marginal.
